mcqs.question: A company wants to hide which internal employee made a request before it reaches the public internet. What should sit in front of the client?
options: An API gateway, because it always encrypts client traffic
A reverse proxy — it hides backend servers from clients, which is the opposite direction
A forward proxy — it represents the client to external servers, hiding the client's identity
A CDN, since it caches content close to the client
mcqs.explanation: A forward proxy is specifically the client-facing pattern that hides client identity from destinations. A reverse proxy solves the opposite problem, and neither an API gateway nor a CDN is defined by hiding client identity.

mcqs.question: What's the main reason to terminate TLS at a reverse proxy rather than at every individual backend server?
options: It automatically load-balances requests regardless of backend health
It's the only way HTTPS can be used at all
It removes the need for DNS resolution
Certificate management and encryption/decryption CPU cost live in one place instead of being duplicated across every backend
mcqs.explanation: Centralizing cert management and encryption overhead is the concrete benefit. HTTPS works fine terminated anywhere; TLS termination doesn't affect DNS resolution or provide health-aware load balancing by itself.

mcqs.question: What distinguishes an API gateway from a plain reverse proxy?
options: It adds application-aware policy like authentication, rate limiting, and request routing/aggregation on top of basic proxying
It cannot terminate TLS, unlike a reverse proxy
It only works with GraphQL APIs, not REST
It replaces the need for backend servers entirely
mcqs.explanation: Application-aware policy (auth, rate limiting, aggregation) is the actual distinguishing feature. API gateways typically do terminate TLS, work with any API style, and still route to real backends.

mcqs.question: Why do reverse proxy and load balancer often refer to the same piece of software in practice?
options: Load balancers are a legacy technology fully replaced by reverse proxies
A reverse proxy fronting multiple interchangeable backends is, by definition, doing load balancing — the terms describe overlapping roles, not separate products
Reverse proxies cannot distribute traffic across more than one backend
They're unrelated concepts that happen to share deployment tools by coincidence
mcqs.explanation: The roles genuinely overlap — a reverse proxy in front of many backends is performing load balancing. Neither is obsolete or incapable of the other's job; the overlap is structural, not coincidental.
